oneLineAnswer: A quick-relief inhaled medicine that relaxes tight airway muscles so breathing gets easier during asthma symptoms.
whatItIs: Salbutamol and albuterol are two names for the same medicine. Chemically it is a small molecule with the formula C13H21NO3. It is a bronchodilator, meaning a medicine that widens the breathing tubes. It belongs to the drug family called beta-adrenergic agonists.
whatItDoes: It relaxes the smooth muscle wrapped around your airways, so narrowed breathing tubes open up.
The drug switches on beta-2 adrenergic receptors, docking sites on airway muscle, and that signal ends in relaxation.
Labels approve it for treating or preventing bronchospasm, the sudden tightening of airway muscles, in people aged 4 and older.
It is also approved to prevent the airway tightening that exercise can set off.
It is a rescue medicine: it opens airways during symptoms and does not calm inflamed airways.
howPeopleUseIt: Most people inhale it, as a metered-dose inhaler, a dry powder inhaler, or a solution used in a nebulizer.
Quick-relief medicine like this is normally carried all the time, so it is at hand when symptoms start.
Some inhalers pair albuterol with a second drug, such as ipratropium or the steroid budesonide.
Because asthma differs between people, a clinician decides whether this medicine fits, and starting asthma medicine without that advice is not recommended.

commonSideEffects: In trials, the most common complaints were throat irritation, viral respiratory infections, upper airway inflammation, cough, and muscle pain.
A shaky feeling in the hands, called tremor, is a known effect of this drug family.
Palpitations, a fast heartbeat, dizziness, headache, restlessness and trouble sleeping have been reported.
Potassium in the blood can drop, and blood sugar can change.
seriousSigns: Rarely the medicine does the opposite of its job. Labels call this paradoxical bronchospasm, breathing that gets worse right after a dose.
Immediate allergic reactions are possible, including rash, swelling, low blood pressure, and the severe whole-body reaction called anaphylaxis.
Very large amounts have been linked to deaths in people with asthma.
Heart effects appear in some people: pulse or blood pressure changes, chest pain, and irregular rhythms.
Needing the inhaler more often than usual can be a marker of asthma that is getting worse.
whoShouldAvoid: Anyone with a known allergy to an ingredient in the product should not use it.
Labels advise care in people with underlying heart disease, especially poor coronary blood flow, irregular heartbeats, or high blood pressure.
Care is also advised with seizure disorders, an overactive thyroid, or diabetes.
People with asthma are normally not given beta-blockers, a different drug class that can set off severe airway tightening.
Use in children younger than 4 years is not established.

interactions: Beta-blockers can cancel the airway-opening effect and can trigger severe bronchospasm in asthma.
Water pills that are not potassium-sparing can worsen heart-rhythm changes and low potassium when combined with this drug.
In one small study of healthy volunteers, albuterol lowered blood digoxin levels by roughly 16 to 22 percent.
Monoamine oxidase inhibitors and tricyclic antidepressants call for extreme caution, because the effect on blood vessels can be increased.
Other short-acting inhaled bronchodilators of the same type are not meant to be used alongside it.
pregnancyAndChildren: Nobody has run a randomized trial of albuterol in pregnancy. Observational studies and case reports have not consistently linked inhaled albuterol to birth defects or miscarriage, but those studies have design limits. In animals, high doses caused cleft palate in mice and delayed bone formation in rabbits. Asthma that is poorly controlled in pregnancy carries its own risks to mother and baby, so labels say pregnant women with asthma should be closely monitored. The medicine is not approved for stopping preterm labor. It has not been measured in breast milk, and trials in children under 4 did not show it worked, so its use in that age group is not established.
whatWeDoNotKnow: There are no randomized studies of albuterol in pregnancy, so the pregnancy picture rests on weaker observational evidence.
No data exist on how much albuterol passes into breast milk.
Labels state that the clinical relevance of the heart-rhythm changes seen on ECG is unknown.
It is unclear whether the fall in digoxin levels matters for people who take both drugs long term.
Whether this drug alone controls asthma is unsettled; labels note a single bronchodilator may not be adequate for many people.
This record says nothing about liver injury, because the LiverTox chapter could not be retrieved.

gaps: The openFDA query on the name Salbutamol returned HTTP 404. The english generic_name and substance_name fields use albuterol, so every label section came from the albuterol queries instead.
NCCIH has no albuterol page: https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/albuterol returned HTTP 404, so no NCCIH content is used here.
The LiverTox chapter (NCBI Bookshelf NBK548313) was blocked by a reCAPTCHA check and could not be read, so no liver-injury information appears in this record.
The PubChem web page returned only the title line, so identity data came from the PubChem REST API (PUG View) rather than the rendered page.
No dose, timing, or personal protocol is given here; that is a deliberate editorial rule, not a data gap.
No human milk transfer data were found in any fetched source.
Nothing was retrieved on long-term daily use of albuterol by people who do not have asthma, or on non-medical use, so no claim is made about either.
MedlinePlus drug monographs, Examine, Labdoor, MSKCC, ConsumerLab, WebMD, Healthline, Drugs.com and RxList were not fetched or cited.
summary: This record covers what salbutamol (albuterol) is, how it opens airways as a quick-relief beta-agonist bronchodilator, its common and serious effects, its drug interactions, and what the label does and does not say about pregnancy, breastfeeding and young children.
